unit.title: Git in depth
unit.description: Commits and the staging area, branches, merge and rebase, conflicts, pull requests and review, revert versus reset, stash, tags, good commit messages, history

cards.definition: Git has three places: your files (working tree), the changes chosen for the next commit (staging area, filled by git add) and the history (repository, written by git commit).
cards.example: Edit two files, git add only one, commit: the other stays modified but not committed.

cards.definition: A movable pointer to a commit, used to work on a feature without touching main. Creating one is instant; you switch with git switch.

Both bring the commits of one branch into another. Merge keeps both histories and adds a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of the target, giving a straight history. Never rebase commits others already pulled.
cards.example: git rebase main on your own feature branch before opening a pull request.

cards.definition: When two branches changed the same lines, Git cannot choose and marks the file with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>. You edit the file to the right version, then git add and continue.
cards.example: Two people changed the same headline in index.html.

cards.definition: A request to merge a branch, on GitHub or GitLab, where teammates review the diff, comment and automated checks (tests, lint) run before merging.
cards.example: A PR titled Add pricing page with screenshots and a green CI.

cards.definition: git revert creates a new commit that undoes an old one: safe on shared branches. git reset moves the branch pointer back and can drop commits: only for local, unshared work.
cards.example: A bad commit is on main: git revert <sha>, then push.

cards.definition: Puts your uncommitted changes aside so you can switch branches with a clean tree, then git stash pop brings them back.
cards.example: An urgent fix on main while your feature is half done.

cards.definition: A short summary line in the imperative (Add, Fix, Remove) under about 50 characters, then a blank line and the why if needed. Small commits that each do one thing.
cards.example: Fix the tax rounding on invoices over 1,000 euros

exercises.prompt: You edited three files and want to commit only one. Which command comes first?
choices: git add that-file.js
git commit -a
git push origin main
git reset --hard
exercises.explain: git add puts chosen changes in the staging area; git commit records only what is staged.

exercises.prompt: What does git switch -c landing do?
choices: Creates the landing branch and moves onto it
Deletes the landing branch everywhere
Merges landing into the current branch
Renames the current branch to landing
exercises.explain: It is the modern form of git checkout -b. git branch landing would only create it.

exercises.prompt: A bad commit was pushed to main and colleagues pulled it. How do you undo it?
choices: git revert with the commit id, then push
git reset --hard to before it, then force push
Delete the repository and clone it again
Edit the files by hand without committing
exercises.explain: revert adds a new commit that cancels the old one, so nobody history is rewritten. Force pushing a reset on shared work breaks others.

exercises.prompt: What do these markers in a file mean?
choices: A merge conflict to resolve by hand
A comment syntax used by Git
A file that Git ignores
A tag marking a release
exercises.explain: Keep the right version (or a mix), remove the markers, then git add the file and finish the merge.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about rebase is true?
choices: Never rebase commits that others already pulled
Rebase is always safer than merge
Rebase deletes the branch you rebase onto
Rebase only works on the main branch
exercises.explain: Rebase rewrites commits. On your own unpushed branch it gives a clean history; on shared history it creates chaos.

exercises.prompt: You must fix a bug on main but your feature branch has unfinished changes. What is the quickest clean move?
choices: git stash, switch to main, fix, come back, git stash pop
Commit the broken work directly on main
Delete your changes and rewrite them later
Copy the files to the desktop as a backup
exercises.explain: stash keeps work aside without polluting the history.

choices: Fix tax rounding on invoices over 1,000 euros
fix
changes
Updated stuff and fixed things and more
exercises.explain: Imperative, specific, short. Future you will search the history with these words.

exercises.prompt: A pull request lets teammates review the changes and lets automated tests run before merging.
exercises.explain: True. Review plus CI catches bugs and shares knowledge. Many teams protect main so that only reviewed, green PRs can merge.

choices: The commit history, one short line per commit
Only the files changed since yesterday
The list of all remote branches
The password used for GitHub
exercises.explain: Each line shows the short commit id and the summary. Add --graph to see branches and merges.

exercises.prompt: What does git tag v1.5.0 do?
choices: Gives a permanent name to the current commit, for a release
Creates a new branch called v1.5.0
Uploads the code to the app store
Changes the version number in package.json
exercises.explain: Tags mark releases. Push them with git push origin v1.5.0; CI pipelines often build on tags.

exercises.prompt: Put a typical feature workflow in order.
steps: Commit small changes as you work
Open a pull request and get a review
Merge once CI is green, then delete the branch
exercises.explain: Branch, commit, push, review, merge. Short-lived branches mean fewer conflicts.
The local branch is feature/pricing, not pricing: Git answers that the src refspec pricing does not match any. Push the real branch name.
